name: Awngi
confidence_why: Hetzron (1969, 1976, 1997) describes a penultimate demarcative stress operating alongside tone, Worku Gela (1986) instead puts stress on the first syllable (final in adjectives, adverbs and imperatives), and Joswig (2010), the fullest phonology of the language, treats Awngi as a two-level tone language and could not confirm any independent stress, so first-hand descriptions disagree on whether Awngi has word stress at all and, if it does, where it falls.

tone_statements.quote: Hetzron (1997: 483) describes Awngi as having stress independent of tone. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is accompanied by a slight rise in pitch. However, Joswig's more detailed study (2009) analyses Awngi as a tone language and cannot confirm the stress that Hetzron observed. ... A large part of the Awngi lexicon contains words that have no pitch change and no stress (Joswig 2009: 1422-1423).

tone_statements.summary: Secondary/comparative: Awngi counted as a Cushitic tone language (prominence by pitch); conflicting primary reports on an additional penultimate stress (Hetzron yes, Joswig not confirmed); many lexical words toneless/all-low.

tone_statements.quote: All this leads to the conclusion that the low tone of Hetzron and Palmer really is just a phonetic variation of the mid tone, reserved for the vowel /a/ on open utterance-final syllables. Therefore it is reasonable to claim that there are only two phonemic tone levels in Awngi, high and low. ... The conflicting evidence from Hetzron and Worku certainly makes it questionable whether there is any stress of intensity in Awngi at all. It has not been observed in the data collected for this study. ... The fact, however, that not only roots but most affixes bear their own tones speaks strongly against such an analysis. Finally, the occurrence of floating tones makes any pitch-accent analysis very difficult to maintain.

sources.quote: 'We can observe that stress is placed either on the first syllable or on the final syllable' (p.56); rule: stress on the first syllable by default; 'if the word is polysyllabic and together with the grammatical category it belongs [adjective, adverb, or imperative], its final syllable will be stressed' (p.57); 'Thus, if stress is predictable, we can conclude it is nonphonemic (or fixed) in Awngi' (p.57); final stress 'is accompanied by the concomitant lengthening (fortition) of the onset consonant' (p.58). Summary p.63: 'five suprasegments (a stress and four tone levels) ... two tonemes'. Exam

sources.note: Third primary on Awngi prosody, not in the record: gives predictable non-phonemic stress on the FIRST syllable (final for polysyllabic adjectives/adverbs/imperatives) alongside four tone levels — a location incompatible with Hetzron's penult, reinforcing the conflict classification; should be added to the primary-stress rule/contra.

sources.quote: 'By all definitions above, Kulazngi is a tone language, or it is not a mere pitch-accent language, because every syllable in a word bears low, mid, or high tone having a lexical as well as a grammatical function' (p.44); 'Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones' (p.45). No word-stress statement anywhere in the phonology chapter (only mention of stress: 'Kemanteney has only stress (Hetzron 1976)'); no penultimate/initial prominence rule given.
sources.note: Glottolog's only 'grammar' for awng1244 (Kunfäl/Kulisi dialect); its phonology chapter describes H/M/L + HL tone with lexical and grammatical function and gives no word-stress rule — silent on stress, consistent with Joswig's tone-only analysis.

sources.locator: p.1421 (section following Fig. 2, before 'The Falling Tone'); p.1422 'Factors Suggesting a pitch accent Interpretation'; p.1424 'Conclusion'
sources.note: Argues Palmer's and Hetzron's four tones (H, M, L, falling) reduce to two phonemic levels H and L (their low = phonetic variant of mid on utterance-final open /a/); falling = H+L on one word-final syllable, derived by floating-tone rules (Rule 1 floating tone assignment, Rule 2 H-floating + final L -> fall), no rising tones; weighs a pitch accent analysis and rejects it because most affixes carry their own tones and floating tones occur; stress of intensity (Hetzron penult vs Worku initial/final) 'not observed in the data collected for this study'.
